rubric.GT core conclusion: Fig. 2f compares the jump and noise epochs by plotting, for each fish, kappa from von Mises fits of the scene-bump offset histogram, together with the shuffle median and 95th percentile as chance references. The bump phase remained significantly aligned to the scene orientation in many more fish during the jump epoch than during the noise epoch, with 14 out of 24 fish above chance in jump and only 3 out of 24 in noise, indicating that recognizable landmark cues were much more effective than optic flow alone for maintaining a stable scene-relative offset.

Scoring items.criterion: States that Fig. 2f compares the jump and noise epochs for each fish
Scoring items.deduction_rule: Deduct 15 points if the jump-versus-noise comparison is missing or reversed. Deduct 6-8 points if both conditions are mentioned but their role as the main comparison is unclear.

Scoring items.criterion: Identifies that the plotted quantity is kappa from von Mises fits of the scene-bump offset histogram (i.e., a concentration/alignment-strength measure)
Scoring items.deduction_rule: Deduct 20 points if the answer does not identify the plotted quantity at all. Deduct 8-12 points if it preserves the idea of an alignment-strength metric but omits kappa or von Mises. Deduct 15-20 points if it misidentifies what is plotted.

Scoring items.criterion: States that significance is assessed relative to a shuffle-based reference (shuffle median and 95th percentile) or equivalent above-chance threshold
Scoring items.deduction_rule: Deduct 15 points if the shuffle/chance reference is omitted entirely. Deduct 5-8 points if significance is mentioned but the shuffle reference or 95th-percentile threshold is not made explicit.

Scoring items.criterion: Reports the key scientific result that stable scene-bump alignment was much stronger / more prevalent in the jump epoch than in the noise epoch, with 14 out of 24 fish above chance in jump versus 3 out of 24 in noise (or a close approximation preserving the large asymmetry)
Scoring items.deduction_rule: Deduct 40 points if the jump-versus-noise comparison is missing or reversed. Deduct 15-20 points if the qualitative contrast is preserved (e.g., 'many more fish in jump than in noise') but the 14/24 vs 3/24 numerical contrast is missing. Deduct 20-30 points if the numbers are substantially incorrect or reversed.

Scoring items.criterion: Preserves the biological interpretation that recognizable landmark cues were more sufficient for stable absolute anchoring, whereas optic flow alone was often insufficient to maintain a stable scene-relative offset
Scoring items.deduction_rule: Deduct 10 points only if the answer gives an incorrect interpretation (e.g., claiming noise showed equally or more stable anchoring). Deduct 3-5 points if the interpretation is omitted but the core quantitative result is preserved.

Acceptable deviations: Paraphrasing 'scene-bump alignment' as 'stable alignment to the scene', 'kept a stable scene-relative offset', or 'maintained anchoring to scene orientation' is acceptable if the meaning is preserved
Referring to kappa as 'concentration', 'offset consistency', or 'alignment strength' is acceptable if the statistical meaning is preserved
Omitting exact wording such as '95th percentile' is acceptable if the answer clearly conveys above-chance, shuffled, or bootstrap-based significance
Reporting the result approximately (e.g., 'about half the fish in jump versus only a few in noise') is acceptable for partial credit
Omitting figure-display details such as dot colors, layout, or plotting style is acceptable
rubric.Scoring instructions: Full credit requires capturing what the figure plots (kappa from von Mises fits of scene-bump offset), the jump-versus-noise comparison, the shuffle-based chance reference, the main numerical contrast (14/24 vs 3/24 fish above chance), and the biological interpretation regarding landmark cues versus optic flow. Partial credit should be given when the answer preserves the main trend and contrast but simplifies numbers, omits the metric name, or omits the broader interpretation. Low scores should be assigned when the answer reverses the direction of the effect, omits the jump-vs-noise comparison, misidentifies what is plotted, fails to preserve the above-chance nature of the test, or reduces the panel to a generic visual description.
